concepts.offTopic: If an n-type semiconductor has a huge excess of mobile electrons compared to holes, does that mean the material as a whole is negatively charged?

concepts.subject: physics
concepts.lessonTitleHint: Extrinsic Semiconductors: Doping and Carrier Types
concepts.misconception: I think n-type material should be negatively charged overall, since it has extra mobile electrons
concepts.correctTyped: No — every donor atom that releases its extra electron becomes a fixed, immobile positive ion, exactly balancing the mobile electron charge; the material remains exactly electrically neutral overall
concepts.wrongTyped: Yes — n-type material should be negatively charged overall, since it has extra mobile electrons

concepts.offTopic: If you double the forward voltage applied to a diode (while staying above its turn-on voltage), does the current through it also roughly double, the way it would for a simple resistor following Ohm's law?

concepts.subject: physics
concepts.misconception: I think a diode should behave like a resistor once it is conducting, so doubling the voltage should roughly double the current
concepts.correctTyped: No — a diode's forward current rises roughly exponentially with voltage past the turn-on threshold; doubling the voltage can increase current by a much larger factor than two
concepts.wrongTyped: Yes — a diode should behave like a resistor once it is conducting, so doubling the voltage should roughly double the current
